bib.title: Recipes for Building an Open-Domain Chatbot

legacy_report:
SOURCE: Recipes for Building an Open-Domain Chatbot. Stephen Roller, Emily Dinan, Naman Goyal, Da Ju, Mary Williamson, Yinhan Liu, Jing Xu, Myle Ott, Kurt Shuster, Eric M. Smith, Y-Lan Boureau, Jason Weston (Facebook AI Research). EACL 2021, pages 300–325. arXiv 2004.13637. This is the BlenderBot paper.

COVERAGE: I read all 96,354 of 96,354 extracted characters across all 26 pages, including Appendices A–H, every results table and the failure-case figures. I skimmed the references only to trace where the methods come from. The text in conversation-screenshot figures (Figs 1, 6, A.16–A.18, A.20, A.22) is images and did not extract. Only the captions came through. The text of Figs A.15 and A.21 did extract.

BOTTOM LINE ON RETRIEVAL: The paper has little to say about retrieval, and what it says is mostly negative. Retrieve-and-refine is a side experiment. Once generator decoding was tuned, neither the dialogue-retrieval version nor the Wikipedia-knowledge version beat the plain generator on human engagingness. The authors call their retrieval experiments "inconclusive". The parts most useful to the course are the hallucination examples, where Wiz Generative gets a fact right and the non-retrieval model invents one, the alpha-blending trick, and the decoding and length findings.

CLAIMS
- claim: With the best decoding settings, retrieve-and-refine (both the dialogue and the knowledge version) did not beat the plain generator on human ratings.
  number: none (see Fig 2 rows below)
  setup: BST fine-tuned models, human-bot ACUTE-Eval of engagingness, 100 crowdworker conversations of 14+ turns per model
  quote: "We ﬁnd RetNRef models (both dialogue version and using knowledge retrieval) do not improve over their gen-erative counterparts when using the best decoding schemes for the generative models"
  where: p5
- claim: RetNRef's earlier advantage disappeared once decoding was tuned. The authors suspect it only came from producing longer outputs.
  number: none
  setup: footnote 8, against the self-chat result in Fig A.5
  quote: "after optimizing the generative model decoding parameters, decoding length and beam blocking, it then performs much better compared to RetNRef. The RetNRef model produces longer generations than the vanilla greedy-search generation algo-rithms, so the original improvement may be from this."
  where: p5 fn 8
- claim: Adding Wikipedia knowledge retrieval made human ratings slightly worse than a same-size model without it.
  number: Wiz Generative 2.7B 47 vs human 53; BST Generative 2.7B 49 vs 51 (engagingness against human-human logs, neither significant)
  setup: Fig 2. 2.7B models, TF-IDF over Wikipedia, then a poly-encoder that picks one sentence
  quote: "Unfortunately the read-ing of knowledge only had a negative impact in ACUTE-Evals compared to a similarly sized model without knowledge retrieval (Figure 2). This might reﬂect both (i) deeper knowledge rarely being re-quired in the current evaluation setup; and (ii) the model attempting to use knowledge when there is no need, or using it incorrectly."
  where: p7
- claim: Against Meena, Wiz Generative also scored below the plain BST generator.
  number: engagingness 61 vs 75; humanness 59 vs 65
  setup: Figs A.14 and 3, human-chat ACUTE-Eval against Meena's public logs
  quote: "Wiz Generative (2.7B) 61 ∗∗ 39 ∗∗" / "BST Generative (2.7B) 75 ∗∗ 25 ∗∗"
  where: p22 (Fig A.14), p6 (Fig 3)
- claim: The authors give hallucination as the reason for knowledge retrieval, and their own probes show it working. The non-retrieval model invented biographies that Wiz Generative got right from Wikipedia.
  number: none
  setup: author-constructed probes, Fig A.20
  quote: "Wojciech Zaremba is an AI Researcher born in Poland, and Amon Tobin is a Brazilian elec-tronic musician, which the Wiz Generative model re-trieves from Wikipedia correctly (last two examples). The Generative BST 2.7B model which does not use retrieval instead hallucinates an Italian football player and an American singer."
  where: p25
- claim: Factual errors were rare in the crowdworker evaluation because the chats were too shallow to test knowledge.
  number: none
  setup: open-ended chats that start with "Hi!" and run 14 turns
  quote: "Perhaps surprisingly, factual errors appear relatively rarely in crowdworker con-versations with the bots. We believe this is due to the nature of the evaluation conducted"
  where: p7
- claim: Alpha-blending stops the generator from ignoring the retrieved utterance: during training, the retrieved response is replaced by the gold one alpha% of the time. Knowledge retrieval did not need it.
  number: alpha = 0.5 in the experiments
  setup: Appendix B.3. Knowledge RetNRef trains on gold knowledge only
  quote: "a trained model often opts to sim-ply ignore the retrieval utterance, as was shown in Weston et al. (2018). To ensure it is used, one can replace the retrieved response instead with the gold responseα% of the time"
  where: p13–14
- claim: In self-chat with untuned decoding, RetNRef beat the plain generator, but pure retrieval beat both.
  number: RetNRef 60 vs Generative 40; Retrieval 67 vs Generative 33
  setup: Fig A.5. 90M generator, 256M poly-encoder, beam 10, no minimum length, alpha = 0.5
  quote: "Retrieve and Reﬁne ( α = 0 .5) outperforms its Generative (90M, beam search decoding) but not its Retrieval (256M) counterpart"
  where: p19
- claim: In human-bot chat with tuned decoding, both RetNRef and the generator beat pure retrieval. RetNRef against the generator was not significant.
  number: RetNRef 56 vs Generative 44 (not significant); Generative 71 vs Retrieval 29
  setup: Fig A.13. 90M generator with minimum beam length 20
  quote: "All results are signiﬁcant ( p < 0.01) except for RetNRef vs. Generative."
  where: p21
- claim: Setting a minimum beam length was the largest decoding win measured. 20 BPE tokens was best.
  number: 83% vs 17%
  setup: Fig A.6. 2.7B generator, self-chat engagingness, about 140 trials per pair
  quote: "Min. Length 20 83 ∗∗ 17 ∗∗"
  where: p20 (summary on p4)
- claim: Response length tracks engagement. With the constraint, outputs averaged about 21 tokens, against 9.5 without it and 18.0 for humans.
  number: 21.3 vs 9.5; Meena 10.4; human 18.0
  setup: Fig 4, 8k BPE tokens
  quote: "Generative BST (2.7B) with the constraint (of 20) is around 21 tokens, vs. 9.5 to-kens without. Thus, the beam search often ends as soon as the constraint is fulﬁlled."
  where: p6
- claim: Beam size 10 was a sweet spot and roughly matched sampling. Nothing in this comparison was significant.
  number: 48% to 52%
  setup: Fig A.8. Top-k with k=40, sample-and-rank with 20 samples
  quote: "a value of 10 is superior to 1 or 30, which is then on par with sampling methods (48% to 52%), although none of these results is signiﬁ-cant"
  where: p4
- claim: Lower perplexity did not mean better human ratings. The 9.4B model lost to the 2.7B model on engagingness.
  number: 56% win for 2.7B; perplexity 8.6 vs 9.0 (Table 3)
  setup: direct ACUTE-Eval of engagingness, 2.7B vs 9.4B
  quote: "which resulted in a 56% win for the smaller model"
  where: p5
- claim: RetNRef had slightly worse perplexity than the plain generator.
  number: 9.8 vs 9.0 (2.7B); 14.2 vs 13.8 (90M)
  setup: Table 3, average over the BST validation sets
  quote: "2.7B 12.0 9.0 9.8"
  where: p5
- claim: Even the best model overuses stock phrases. Unlikelihood training cut the repeats but did not help engagingness.
  number: "Do you have" 110 (MLE) / 60 (UL) / 6 (human)
  setup: Fig 5, 100 crowdworker conversations, 2.7B model
  quote: "Do you have 110 60 6"
  where: p7
- claim: Headline result against Meena.
  number: 75/25 engagingness, 65/35 humanness
  setup: BST Generative 2.7B with tuned beam search against Meena's public logs
  quote: "75% to 25% in terms of engagingness, and by 65% to 35% in terms of humanness (both statistically signiﬁcant, two-tailed binomial test,p< 0.01)"
  where: p1

LIMITS: Evaluation used 14-turn open chats that start with "Hi!", which the authors say rarely probe knowledge. So the paper does not show whether retrieval helps when a conversation needs facts. The context limit is 128 BPE tokens. Knowledge retrieval conditions on a single sentence picked from TF-IDF candidates. Hallucination is never measured systematically: the evidence is cherry-picked or author-built examples (Fig A.20). The authors concede the retrieval and unlikelihood experiments are "inconclusive". The evaluation is English chit-chat, not QA. Many self-chat differences were not significant. This is 2020-era technology: seq2seq models up to 9.4B parameters, no instruction tuning, no dense retrieval over passages.

BUILDS ON: Weston et al., 2018 (Retrieve and Refine, alpha-blending); Dinan et al., 2019c (Wizard of Wikipedia knowledge retrieval); Humeau et al., 2019 (poly-encoder); Welleck et al., 2020 and Li et al., 2019a (unlikelihood); Li et al., 2019b (ACUTE-Eval); Smith et al., 2020 (Blended Skill Talk); Paulus et al., 2017 (n-gram blocking); Fan et al., 2018 (top-k); Adiwardana et al., 2020 (Meena, sample-and-rank); Holtzman et al., 2019 (degeneration); Massarelli et al., 2019 (hallucination in generation).

CODE: None. The paper contains only equations: MLE, and unlikelihood L_ULE = L_MLE + αL_UL on p14.

FIGURES:
- First choice: Figure 2 (p6), the engagingness ACUTE-Eval table against human logs. In one table it shows BST RetNRef 2.7B (46/54) and Wiz Generative (47/53) landing next to the plain BST Generative 2.7B (49/51), and std-beam variants far below at 21/79. It makes the point that decoding mattered more than retrieval faster than prose would.
- Second choice: Figure A.6 (p20), minimum beam length 5/10/20/40 against unconstrained (52, 68, 83, 82), for 06 § Sampling.
- Fig A.20, the hallucinated biographies, is the most vivid, but it is a screenshot and its text did not extract.

FIT WITH THE NOTES:
- Best fit: 02-why-rag-and-the-augmented-prompt.md § "What RAG buys you", the "Fewer hallucinations" row (line 111). The paper supports the mechanism with the Fig A.20 examples. It adds an honest counterweight: knowledge retrieval lowered human ratings in shallow chat, possibly because the model used knowledge "when there is no need, or using it incorrectly". That fits as a sharpens citation, or a Pitfalls line: "retrieval can hurt when the task doesn't need knowledge". It does not contradict the Shuster et al. 68.2% to 8–21% figure. Different eval, and no hallucination rate is measured here.
- Second fit: 06-generation-for-rag.md § Sampling. The notes have no beam search, minimum-length or n-gram-blocking rows. The paper supports the existing "Greedy ... can loop and repeat" and repetition-penalty rows; n-gram blocking is its counterpart. It adds a beam-versus-sampling finding: the paper says it runs "contrary to previous work which reports that beam search is inferior to sampling". The notes do not currently claim sampling beats beam, so there is no conflict.
- Also relevant: the alpha-blending fact (generators ignore retrieved text unless training forces them to use it) relates to 06 § "Context against the model's prior", though it concerns training rather than prompting.

PROBLEMS: The conversation-screenshot figures did not extract (text is in images). Some ligatures and hyphenation are broken in the quotes (e.g. "ﬁ", "gen-erative"), copied as extracted. figures.py captions returned only main-body figures 1–6, not the appendix figures. The PDF contained no embedded instructions.
